results.test: user sees the correct total including discount and VAT
results.fixerReasoning: The app returned VAT 294, which is 21% of the full subtotal (1398 × 0.21 = 293.58, rounded to 294). The rule documented in public/cart.js itself and in the test case says VAT is charged after the discount: (1398 − 140) × 0.21 = 264.18, rounded to 264. The test matches the agreed rule. The bug is in `vat()` in public/cart.js, which sets `taxable = subtotal(items)` and never subtracts `discount(items)`.
results.fixerReport: The app charges VAT on the pre-discount subtotal. This breaks business rule 3 in public/cart.js ('VAT ... charged on the amount the customer actually pays, i.e. AFTER the discount has been taken off'). Any customer whose order is over 1000 is overcharged. In this test that's 30 (VAT 294 instead of 264). The total is also wrong: the app shows 1552 where the correct figure is 1522. Suggested app fix, for a developer to review rather than for the test-fixing loop to apply: in `vat()`, change `const taxable = subtotal(items);` to `const taxable = subtotal(items) - discount(items);`. The test should stay as it is and keep failing until the app is fixed. Two unrelated problems turned up while checking this; neither caused this failure. (1) data/products.json lists the desk mat at 349, but the 'catalogue price' test and its test case expect 299. That's possible data drift, and someone needs to decide which price is correct. (2) The 'last product can be added to the cart' test case has no matching test, and its expected subtotal of 349 contradicts the cable sleeve's price of 199.

results.test: user sees the whole catalogue once it has loaded
results.fixerReasoning: In the app, public/index.html renders the first four products straight away and adds the fifth (Cable sleeve) 1500 ms later (`products.slice(0, 4)` now, `products.slice(4)` in a `setTimeout(..., 1500)`). So the app does show all five products in the end. The test fails because it sleeps a fixed 100 ms and then reads `count()` once, without waiting, so it always sees 4. The fix is an assertion that keeps checking until the count reaches 5. A longer sleep would only hide the problem.
results.reviewerReasoning: I checked public/index.html (lines 57-63). It renders products.slice(0, 4) right away and products.slice(4) inside a setTimeout of 1500 ms, with a comment saying the catalogue is paged on purpose. So the app does show all five products, and the test failed only because it slept 100 ms and then read count() once. The new toHaveCount(5) assertion keeps retrying until the count is 5. That fixes the race without a hardcoded sleep, and it still requires exactly five products, the same as the reference data.
reviewerConcerns: Playwright's default expect timeout is 5 s and the delay is 1.5 s, so there is enough headroom. If the app's delay grows past 5 s, the test will fail, which is the right outcome.
